# Access as code

![](../images/spot-5.svg){.spot fig-alt="A gate with a yellow lintel, three pods and a sheet of paper on a mint tile; an elephant in a vest checks a clipboard."}
The rules for who may read or write which tables are usually typed into a database by hand, once,
and then nobody remembers why they look the way they do. Writing them down as code fixes that: the
rules live in a file, a tool compares the file with the server, and a change is a reviewed diff. The
lab writes one small access model twice, once with Pulumi and once with pgsesame, and applies each
to a real server to show how the two approaches differ.

## The model

The model is the same in both tools:

- Two group roles that cannot log in: `app_ro` (read) and `app_rw` (read and write).
- Usage on the schema, and grants on its tables and sequences.
- **Default privileges**, so tables that the `app` role creates later get the same grants
  automatically. Hand-made setups most often forget this part.
- Two login users, `reporter` and `ingest`, who get access only through membership in a group role.

Tables, schemas and extensions are left out. They belong to the application and its migrations.

## Pulumi: state and a diff

`pulumi/__main__.py` builds the model with `pulumi-postgresql`, a bridge to the provider that
Terraform uses. `pulumi preview` compares the program with the last applied state, and `pulumi up`
applies the difference.

```bash
pulumi preview            # what would change
pulumi up
pulumi preview --refresh  # drift check: re-read the database first
```

Running it taught two lessons. First, a plain `preview` compares the program with the *state* file,
not with the database, so changes made by hand show up only with `--refresh`. Second, the grants
have to be chained with `depends_on`. The provider runs them in parallel, and Postgres then fails
with "tuple concurrently updated".

## pgsesame: one YAML file, no state

[pgsesame](https://github.com/almostly/pgsesame) declares the same model in `pgsesame/spec.yaml`.
It keeps no state file. Instead, `plan` reads the database catalog and prints the SQL that would make
the server match the spec.

```yaml
principals:
  app_ro:
    type: role
    privileges:
      schemas: {usage: [public]}
      tables: {select: [public.*]}
  reporter:
    type: user
    password_env: SESAME_REPORTER_PASSWORD
    member_of: [app_ro]

default_privileges:
  - owner: app
    schema: public
    grantee: app_ro
    tables: [select]
```

```bash
sesame plan     # exit code 2 means there are changes
sesame apply    # one transaction: 32 statements on a fresh server
sesame plan     # empty: nothing drifted
sesame import   # write a spec from what a server grants today
```

Destructive changes (revokes, drops and changes of owner) need explicit flags. Passwords come from
environment variables and never from the file.

## Side by side

| | Pulumi | pgsesame |
|---|---|---|
| source of truth | a Python program plus a state file | one YAML spec |
| drift | detected with `--refresh` | every plan reads the database |
| apply | resources in parallel, chained by hand | one transaction |
| scope | anything with a provider, databases and beyond | Postgres roles and privileges |
| secrets | encrypted in stack config | environment variables |

Either tool works, but only one of them should manage the roles on a given server. Pulumi fits when
database access is one part of a larger infrastructure program. pgsesame fits when the database is
the whole story and you want the plan to be SQL you can read.

In the lab, `just sesame plan pg18` and `just sesame apply pg18` run pgsesame, and `pulumi/` holds
the Pulumi stack.
